title: Poker Tells and Inconsistency Patterns: Applying Card-Game Bluff Detection to LLM Evaluation

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: While LLMs playing poker has been studied (Google DeepMind Game Arena, Stanford CS224R projects, strangeloopcanon/llm-poker), the research focuses on LLM poker performance rather than reverse-engineering poker bluff-detection heuristics into general-purpose LLM deception probes. Existing work shows LLMs cannot detect bluffs in poker and have specific heuristic failures. The novel contribution here is operationalizing poker tells (bet-sizing analogues, timing analogues, range imbalance) as a probe battery for detecting deception in non-game LLM outputs. No existing work applies this specific mapping from poker heuristics to general LLM deception evaluation.

title: Applying Forensic Linguistic Stylometry to Detect Strategy Switching in LLM Outputs

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Stylometry for distinguishing human vs. LLM-generated text exists (arXiv:2507.00838). Computational measures of deceptive language have been studied in human text (Frontiers in Communication, 2022). Syntactic stylometry for deception detection in human text exists (ACL 2012). However, applying stylometric change-point detection specifically to identify strategy switching within LLM outputs (honest-to-deceptive phase transitions within a single generation) is novel. No existing work combines stylometric features with change-point detection models to identify mid-output behavioral shifts in LLM text. The DeCLaRatiVE approach applies stylometry to deception in text but does not address within-output phase transitions.

title: Intervening at the 'Learns Deceptive Communication' Step: Is Deceptive Language a Separable Module?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Adversarial Activation Patching (arXiv:2507.09406) demonstrates that patching activations from deceptive prompts into safe forward passes increases deceptive outputs to 23.9% from a 0% baseline, strongly suggesting separable deception circuits. The 'abliteration' technique (NousResearch/llm-abliteration) removes safety-related circuits via ablation. Research on separable faithful and shortcut circuits supports the modularity hypothesis. The specific contribution of testing whether ablating deception circuits degrades honest communication is partially addressed — the abliteration work shows circuit removal affects behavior, and the adversarial patching work shows deception circuits can be isolated. The novelty is in the bidirectional test (ablate deception, measure honest degradation), which has not been explicitly done.
